name: Self-Adapting Language Models
authors: Adam Zweiger, Jyothish Pari (equal contribution), Han Guo, Ekin Akyürek, Yoon Kim, Pulkit Agrawal; MIT (CSAIL / Improbable AI Lab)
reflection_type: learned-critic-model (the policy itself is RL-trained to generate effective 'self-edits'; the improvement signal is the downstream task reward of the updated model rather than a verbal self-critique). The reflective act is meta-learned self-directed adaptation rather than verbal self-critique of an output.
feedback_source: environment-reward / verifiable downstream performance: the reward is the post-update model's accuracy on the held-out evaluation task (QA accuracy for knowledge incorporation, ground-truth output match for few-shot ARC). Requires ground-truth labels on the downstream task tau to compute the binary improvement reward.
iteration_structure: Nested-loop / episodic: an outer RL loop (ReST-EM rounds) optimizes the self-edit generation policy, and an inner update loop applies the self-edit via SFT (a round of test-time training) and evaluates it. Within the knowledge-incorporation single-passage setting, results are reported after two rounds of ReST-EM. Self-edits are sampled on-policy (M candidates per context).
reflection_object: model weights (primary) plus prompt/context: the model reflects on an input passage/task context and emits a 'self-edit' (synthetic finetuning data + optimization directives such as learning rate, epochs, data augmentations, selective loss over token types); the self-edit is then applied as a persistent gradient-based weight update via SFT. So the modified target is the model's own weights, parameterized through generated training data.
requires_training: nested-RL+SFT: an outer RL loop (ReST-EM = filtered behavior cloning / rejection-sampling + SFT) trains the self-edit generation policy; the inner loop applies SFT to perform the actual weight update. GRPO and PPO were tried but found unstable, so ReST-EM (an EM-style approach) is used.
reward_or_critic_model: verifiable reward: the model itself acts as the policy, and the reward is the measured downstream task performance of the updated model (binary reward = 1 if adaptation via the self-edit improves performance on tau, else 0). No separate trained reward model or learned critic network; relies on ground-truth task labels.
distillation_target: model-weights: reflection/self-edits are distilled into persistent parameter updates (the self-generated synthetic finetuning data is the intermediate artifact, but the durable distillation target is the model's own weights). Stands in contrast to in-context-only methods.
emergent_vs_engineered: engineered/scaffold-trained: the self-edit format is defined per domain via human-designed templates (e.g., 'generate implications' for knowledge incorporation, a JSON config of augmentations/hyperparameters for ARC), and the RL outer loop trains the model to produce effective self-edits within that scaffold. The adaptation behavior is meta-learned via RL rather than RL-emergent in the R1 'aha' sense.
memory_type: model-weights as memory (parametric): there is no external episodic memory store, scratchpad, or skill library; new knowledge/skills are written directly into the weights via self-edits. The self-edit text and synthetic data are transient within an episode.
memory_persistence: cross-task / persistent within the model: weight updates are lasting (the paper demonstrates generalization from single-passage TTT episodes to a continued-pretraining regime with 200 passages, and a continual-learning experiment applying sequential edits). Persistence is in parameters, not an external memory log.
memory_curation_mechanism: overwrite/evolution (self-relinking) via gradient updates with no explicit retention mechanism — this is exactly the weakness the paper flags: repeated self-edits overwrite earlier knowledge (catastrophic forgetting). Curation of which self-edit to keep is done by reward filtering (rejection sampling: reinforce only positive-reward edits; for knowledge incorporation the single best-improving edit is rewarded).
error_localization_granularity: holistic/outcome-level: the reward and self-edit operate at the level of whole-task downstream performance after the weight update (e.g., QA accuracy on a passage, solving an ARC task), not at the step/token level. There is no fine-grained error localization within a reasoning chain.
intra_task_vs_inter_task: inter-task / meta-learning: the RL outer loop learns a general policy for generating self-edits that transfers across task instances (and from single-passage to continued-pretraining and to new ARC tasks). Each adaptation also customizes weights for the specific new input, so it spans both, but the learned skill ('how to self-edit') is inter-task.
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: avoidance-only / forward adaptation: SEAL adapts to incorporate new knowledge or new tasks rather than recovering from a specific failed trajectory mid-flight. It is not a mid-trajectory error-recovery method; improvement comes from selecting and reinforcing higher-reward self-edits in subsequent RL rounds.
task_domains: knowledge incorporation (integrating new factual knowledge from text passages) and few-shot learning / abstract reasoning (few-shot generalization). Broadly: QA/reasoning and decision-making over how to adapt; tool-use is involved in the ARC setting (model invokes augmentation/optimization tools).
benchmarks: SQuAD (no-passage-in-context QA variant, single-passage and continued-pretraining with 200 passages) for knowledge incorporation; a simplified subset of the ARC-AGI benchmark for few-shot learning.
headline_result: On SQuAD no-passage-in-context QA, SEAL improves accuracy from 32.7% (no adaptation; ~33.5% cited in intro) to 47.0% after two rounds of ReST-EM, outperforming finetuning on raw passages and on GPT-4.1-generated synthetic data. On the simplified ARC subset, SEAL reaches a 72.5% success rate vs 0% for ICL and 20% for test-time training with untrained self-edits.
baselines: Knowledge incorporation: no adaptation (base model), finetuning on the raw passage text, finetuning on synthetic data generated by GPT-4.1, and 'Train on Passage + Synthetic' variants (implication-style self-edits without RL). Few-shot ARC: in-context learning (ICL), test-time training with self-edits but without RL training (untrained self-edits), and an oracle TTT upper bound.
gains_vs_baseline: Knowledge incorporation single-passage: +14.3 points QA accuracy over no adaptation (32.7% -> 47.0%), and SEAL's self-generated data beats GPT-4.1-generated synthetic data (a much larger model). Continued-pretraining (200 passages): SEAL highest at 43.8%. Few-shot ARC: 72.5% vs 20% for untrained self-edits (+52.5 points) and vs 0% for ICL.
compute_cost_profile: High training cost: the outer RL loop requires, per candidate self-edit, performing an inner SFT/TTT update and a full downstream evaluation to compute the reward, with M self-edits sampled per context across multiple ReST-EM rounds — i.e., many gradient updates + evaluations per RL step. The paper notes each reward computation involves finetuning and evaluating the model, making the loop expensive; small base models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B for knowledge incorporation, Llama-3.2-1B for ARC) and LoRA/efficient TTT are used to make it tractable. Inference-time adaptation also adds per-task finetuning cost vs a single forward pass. [exact wall-clock/FLOP multipliers not stated as a single number]
known_limitations: (1) Catastrophic forgetting: in the continual-learning experiment, repeated/sequential self-edits degrade performance on earlier tasks as new updates overwrite prior knowledge. (2) Reward computation is expensive (each evaluation requires an inner finetuning + evaluation pass). (3) Requires a paired downstream evaluation task tau with ground-truth labels to compute reward (context-dependent evaluation). (4) Self-edit formats are still human-templated per domain. (5) Demonstrated on relatively small models and a simplified ARC subset.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: oracle-label/ground-truth + env-reward: the RL reward is computed from the updated model's performance on a held-out evaluation set tau (QA answers / ARC ground-truth outputs), so it depends on access to ground-truth task labels (or a verifiable downstream signal). This external supervision is what makes the self-improvement reliable, in contrast to label-free self-consistency methods the authors explicitly critique as fundamentally limited.
self_correction_efficacy: net-positive (with external/verifiable reward): SEAL reliably improves downstream performance because the self-edit policy is selected against a ground-truth-grounded reward, not pure self-judgment. The authors argue self-improvement through interaction with external data is more scalable than self-consistency-based self-improvement. The efficacy is therefore conditioned on having a verifiable downstream signal.
calibration_effect: not-measured: the paper does not report confidence-calibration or 'reasoning tax' metrics; it focuses on task accuracy after adaptation rather than on calibration.
failure_attribution_capability: n/a (SEAL is an adaptation/learning method, not a failure-attribution method; it does not produce a failure taxonomy or attribute errors to steps/agents).
failure_mode_addressed: n/a as a direct target; however the paper itself exposes and discusses a key self-modification failure mode it suffers from: catastrophic forgetting / knowledge overwriting across sequential self-edits (a continual-learning failure), proposing replay, constrained updates, or representational superposition as future mitigations.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: No new reusable benchmark/dataset released; it uses existing resources (SQuAD, a simplified subset of ARC-AGI). Code is released at https://github.com/Continual-Intelligence/SEAL.
builds_on: ReST-EM (Singh et al., 2023, rejection sampling + SFT / EM-style RL); Test-Time Training (TTT) and TTT+ICL for ARC (Akyürek et al., 2024); implication-based knowledge incorporation / synthetic-data finetuning (Akyürek et al.; Lampinen et al.; Park et al.); RL-with-verifiable-reward for LLMs (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-style RLVR) and RLHF; meta-learning and self-referential / self-modifying networks (Schmidhuber line).
extended_by_or_inspired: Follow-up works building directly on SEAL include 'Search over Self-Edit Strategies for LLM Adaptation' (Cheong et al., arXiv:2601.14532, 2026, relaxes SEAL's fixed human self-edit template to let the model generate its own templates with an archive) and 'The Risks of Autonomy: Dynamic Auditing of Self-Editing Language Models in Critical Infrastructure' (DAF-SELM, Myakala et al., SoutheastCon 2026, addressing catastrophic forgetting / alignment drift / data poisoning audit for SEAL-style models).
reasoning_model_native: Not specifically targeting o1/R1-style reasoning models; SEAL is applied to standard instruction-tuned base models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-1B). The framework is model-agnostic, and Future Work envisions models that 'reason about when and how to adapt' and distill chain-of-thought traces into weights, but native reasoning models are not the experimental subject.
on_policy_distillation_link: Strong relevance: SEAL is explicitly on-policy (self-edits are sampled from, and rewards computed with, the current model to avoid stale off-policy triples), and it distills self-generated data into the model's own weights via SFT — effectively a self-distillation / on-policy data-generation loop. It can be viewed as on-policy distillation where the model distills its own RL-selected synthetic edits into parameters, and Future Work proposes distilling CoT traces into weights, closely echoing on-policy distillation / skill-internalization ideas.
sample_efficiency: Knowledge incorporation single-passage results are reported after two rounds of ReST-EM; the ARC few-shot setting adapts from a small number of demonstrations per task. SEAL is trained on single-example TTT episodes yet generalizes to the 200-passage continued-pretraining regime. Each ReST-EM round samples M candidate self-edits per context and reinforces positive-reward (or single best) edits. [exact total number of RL rollouts/gradient steps not reported as a single figure]
